checks.prompt: If important information is missing from the context, what may the model do?

choices.text: Guess
Update its internal weights
Store the missing facts automatically

checks.explanation: Large language models generate outputs conditioned on what they can see. If important information is missing, the model may guess.

provenance.locator: Paragraph P0040
provenance.support: If important information is missing, the model may guess.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Grounding topic, Table 6 row 1
provenance.support: A confident but unsupported answer is marked as a guess.

checks.prompt: Which principle should be checked before blaming the model for a weak answer?

choices.text: Output quality is limited by input quality
Model size is the only cause of a weak answer
More context always improves answer quality
Every weak answer requires fine-tuning

checks.explanation: The chapter’s practical rule is that output quality is limited by input quality. Missing facts, unreliable grounding, conflicting instructions, or missing structure should be diagnosed first.

provenance.locator: Paragraph P0040 and paragraphs P0127-P0128
provenance.support: Output quality is limited by input quality; diagnose context failures before blaming the model.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Diagnose the Context topic, paragraphs P0096-P0102
provenance.support: Pair failure symptoms with likely context causes and the smallest practical fix.

checks.prompt: What does context engineering design?

choices.text: The full information environment the model sees
Only the wording of one instruction
The model’s internal weights

checks.explanation: Prompt engineering focuses on the instruction. Context engineering designs the full information environment, including role, rules, evidence, memory, dynamic facts, examples, format, and the immediate request.

provenance.locator: Paragraphs P0008 and P0028
provenance.support: Context engineering deliberately assembles and organizes the whole input package.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, A Good Prompt Is Not Enough, paragraph P0036
provenance.support: Context engineering designs the full information environment.

checks.prompt: Which package best represents a context-engineered input?

choices.text: Role, rules, evidence, memory, dynamic facts, examples, format, and the request
A single request with no supporting facts or constraints
A training dataset used to update model weights
A hardware upgrade that expands the context window

checks.explanation: An engineered context is a set of components with distinct jobs. The chapter identifies role, constraints, dynamic facts, grounding, memory, profile, tools, examples, output format, and the user request.

provenance.locator: Paragraphs P0071-P0082 and Table 7
provenance.support: Lists the core context components and their purposes.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, A Good Prompt Is Not Enough, paragraphs P0036-P0039
provenance.support: Shows the request inside a labeled context package.

checks.prompt: The context window is best treated as what?

choices.text: Finite working memory measured in tokens
An unlimited archive of every conversation
The maximum length of the model’s answer

checks.explanation: The context window is finite working memory. Everything supplied for the current response consumes tokens, and the model cannot reliably attend to unlimited text.

provenance.locator: Paragraphs P0052-P0054
provenance.support: Defines the context window as finite working memory measured in tokens.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Context Window topic, paragraph P0048 and Table 3 row 2
provenance.support: The context window is finite working memory measured in tokens.

checks.prompt: What can happen when a context nears overload?

choices.text: Distraction, missed instructions, fixation on old details, and verbosity
Every added document improves accuracy in a straight line
The extra text is automatically saved for a later session
The model fine-tunes itself on the oversized prompt

checks.explanation: Even before the hard limit, very large prompts can spread attention thin. The chapter describes distraction, ignored instructions, fixation on older details, and verbose but less accurate outputs.

provenance.locator: Paragraphs P0056-P0058 and Table 6
provenance.support: Describes truncation, reduced quality, and overload symptoms.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Context Window topic, Table 3 row 3
provenance.support: Near overload: distraction, missed instructions, old-detail fixation, and verbosity.

checks.prompt: When context space is limited, what should be protected first?

choices.text: System role, safety or policy rules, and critical constraints
Nice-to-have background
Extra examples before the task and rules

checks.explanation: The token-budget priority table places non-negotiables first: the system role, safety or policy rules, and critical constraints.

provenance.locator: Table 5, priority 1
provenance.support: Non-negotiables: system role plus safety/policy rules plus critical constraints.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Token Budgeting topic, paragraphs P0059-P0063
provenance.support: Protect role and safety rules before lower-priority material.

checks.prompt: Which content belongs last in the token-budget priority order?

choices.text: Nice-to-have background
The user request
Essential grounding facts
Memory required for continuity

checks.explanation: Nice-to-have background is the final priority. The task, essential grounding facts, necessary memory, and required examples or schema receive space first.

provenance.locator: Table 5, priorities 2-6
provenance.support: Nice-to-have background is priority 6.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Token Budgeting topic, Table 4
provenance.support: Rank content from non-negotiables through nice-to-have background.

checks.prompt: Where should the user request appear in the Context Skeleton?

choices.text: Last, after the supporting context
Inside the role block
Before the role and rules

checks.explanation: The chapter’s ordering guidance puts high-priority behavior first and the user request last, so the request is the immediate focus while the preceding blocks provide support.

provenance.locator: Paragraphs P0087-P0089
provenance.support: Role and rules first; dynamic facts and grounding before the request; request last.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Context Skeleton topic, Table 5 row 3
provenance.support: Emphasize behavior and rules first, request last.

checks.prompt: Which sequence follows the chapter’s ordering guidance?

choices.text: Role and rules → dynamic facts and grounding → user request
User request → optional background → role and rules
Mix rules, facts, and the request into one paragraph
Paste the full conversation history before everything else

checks.explanation: A stable order makes the job of each block clear: behavior and constraints first, supporting facts and evidence next, and the immediate request last.

provenance.locator: Table 7 and paragraphs P0083-P0089
provenance.support: Defines the Context Skeleton and ordering guidance.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Context Skeleton topic, paragraphs P0072-P0078
provenance.support: A repeatable skeleton separates blocks and uses an essential sequence.

checks.prompt: What does grounding add to the context?

choices.text: Relevant excerpts from approved sources
New internal model weights
Every available document, whether relevant or not

checks.explanation: Grounding provides relevant reference information, often retrieved from approved sources, so the model can answer from known facts instead of guessing.

provenance.locator: Key term P0021 and paragraphs P0093-P0099
provenance.support: Grounding uses relevant approved excerpts for evidence-bound answers.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Grounding topic, paragraph P0084
provenance.support: Supply the most relevant approved excerpts and require the model to use them.

checks.prompt: Which grounding practice is recommended by the chapter?

choices.text: Find 2–6 short relevant excerpts and require the answer to use them
Paste the entire source document into every request
Rely only on the model’s training memory
Let the model fill missing evidence with plausible details

checks.explanation: The no-code RAG pattern starts with the question, finds 2–6 short relevant excerpts, inserts them into the grounding block, and requires the model to answer from that evidence or say it is insufficient.

provenance.locator: Paragraphs P0096-P0099 and Table 9
provenance.support: Use 2–6 short relevant excerpts; do not dump entire documents.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Grounding topic, Table 6 rows 3-5
provenance.support: Four grounding steps and the smallest sufficient evidence set.

checks.prompt: Which three memory types are taught in Chapter 1?

choices.text: Rolling summary, pinned facts, and retrieval memory
Full transcript, model weights, and output schema
Dynamic facts, system role, and current date

checks.explanation: The chapter identifies three practical memory types: a rolling summary, pinned facts, and retrieval memory.

provenance.locator: Table 10
provenance.support: Rolling summary, pinned facts, and retrieval memory.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Memory topic, paragraphs P0108-P0111
provenance.support: Introduces the same three memory types.

checks.prompt: What should controlled memory carry forward?

choices.text: The decisions, facts, and open items that matter now
Every word from the full conversation
Stale details even when they no longer affect the task
Changing values mixed into the system role

checks.explanation: Controlled memory preserves continuity by carrying forward what matters, while excluding stale or irrelevant conversation. Long raw history is not the same as good memory.

provenance.locator: Paragraph P0103 and Table 10
provenance.support: Maintain a short structured memory block instead of relying on long chat history.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Memory topic, paragraphs P0105-P0114 and Table 8
provenance.support: Carry forward what matters and replace the transcript with a compact memory block.

checks.prompt: Which values belong in a Dynamic Facts block?

choices.text: Date, current status, case ID, deadline, or SLA
The assistant’s permanent persona and tone
The model’s internal weights and layers

checks.explanation: A Dynamic Facts block carries current, case-specific values such as today’s date, status, case ID, deadline, or SLA.

provenance.locator: Paragraphs P0107-P0109
provenance.support: Dynamic facts include current date, ticket status, and SLA.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Dynamic Facts topic, paragraphs P0119-P0123
provenance.support: Current values include date, status, case ID, deadline, and SLA.

checks.prompt: Where should changing case-specific facts be kept?

choices.text: In a separate Dynamic Facts block, apart from the role and durable policies
Inside the permanent role or persona block
Only in a long raw conversation history
Only in model training data

checks.explanation: Changing values should be separated from durable instructions and policies. This makes current-state information easier to update without altering the role or governing rules.

concept.label: Separate current state from durable rules

provenance.locator: Table 11 and paragraphs P0107-P0109
provenance.support: Do not place dynamic facts inside the role/persona block.

provenance.locator: Chapter 1, Dynamic Facts topic, paragraph P0120 and Table 9 rows 4-5
provenance.support: Keep changing facts separate from role and durable policies.

checks.prompt: What does the seven-phase context engineering lifecycle replace?

choices.text: A controlled loop with visible decisions
One-time prompt improvisation based on gut feel
A requirement to use the largest model
Automatic model retraining

checks.explanation: The lifecycle replaces improvised, one-off prompt work with a controlled loop whose decisions, evidence, evaluation, and improvements can be reviewed.

choices.text: Iteration
Selection

A final deployment rollback trigger only

A complete chat-history archive
A larger context window

checks.prompt: What is the main goal of Selection?

choices.text: Choose the smallest set of high-signal information the task actually needs
Preserve every available source to avoid making decisions
Convert all material into one long paragraph
Begin deployment before testing

checks.explanation: Selection keeps the highest-signal context and removes noise, redundancy, stale material, and information that does not help the task.

checks.prompt: Which classification indicates information that can be included only when the task or token budget justifies it?

choices.text: Optional
Always fit
Automatically prohibited

checks.explanation: Selection distinguishes information that always fits, usually fits, or is optional so the context can be adapted without treating all material as equally valuable.

Remove the task and preserve only background
